topic.title: Fat pointers and the engine switch

body.p: JALv3 can compile pointers with a fat representation: a pointer that is stored, passed, or read back through memory carries a tag byte in addition to the address, so one indirect access can reach a variable, a constant array, a pseudo-variable, a routine, or a dynamic string without the compiler deciding at every site.

The engine is on by default since 2026-11-11. A pointer whose binding is known locally is unchanged; only programs that keep a pointer in memory pay for the tag. In the sample tree the 2,850 programs with no stored pointer surface compile byte-identically, and the 90 that exercise one grow by 2.6% of their code.

section.title: Precedence
section.p: Each compile decides the mode in this order:

ol.li: the program's own pragma target fat_pointers;

section.p: The pragma accepts on, off, 3byte and 2byte. off is the per-program opt-out:
3byte and 2byte only choose the 14-bit hybrid pointer width; the 3-byte form is the default there, and 2byte is the RAM-tight alternative.

section.title: Rolling back
section.p: JALV2_FAT_POINTERS=0 restores the classic representation byte for byte in every program that does not set the pragma. That classic mode is deprecated: the compiler prints one JALV2-NOTICE line per compile, and the switch is removed after this release. For a single program use the pragma above; the environment switch is a whole-build escape hatch only.

section.title: Checked switch values
section.p: Every JALV2_* switch follows one rule: an unset or empty value means the default; 1, true, yes and on mean on; 0, false, no and off mean off, case-insensitively and ignoring surrounding whitespace. Any other value is reported once with the code JALV2-SWITCH and the default is used, so a typo cannot flip a mode silently. jalv3-x86-64 --features (alias -v) prints the effective modes before compiling.
